chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from al-Ala' from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar said:

A Muslim slave, a known slave, whom a man had freed, came in with his master to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said, 'O this one, who is this Sinndi?' The man said, 'A known slave, and he was freed by so-and-so.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'I wish I had freed him.'
Then the Sinndi said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I said to my master, 'Free me for seven hundred dirhams, and I will give you three hundred dirhams.'
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'If you had wealth on the day you made the condition, you must give it; and if you did not have wealth on that day, there is nothing upon you.'

key_terms.أَعْتَقَهُ: He freed him (past tense, referring to manumission).
key_terms.اَلْسِّنْدِيُّ: The Sinndi (a nisba indicating origin or characteristic, used here as a name/title).
key_terms.بِعْنِي: Free me (imperative form used in the context of buying freedom).
key_terms.عَارِفٌ: A known or recognized slave, often implying a slave with a specific status or skill.
key_terms.فَلَيْسَ عَلَيْكَ شَيْءٌ: Then there is nothing upon you (no obligation).
key_terms.يَوْمَ شَرَطْتَ: On the day you made the condition/agreement.

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for a freed slave to be obligated to pay the agreed ransom amount?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the juristic principle of *al-istita'ah* (capacity) in manumission contracts, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links the slave's payment obligation to his financial status at the time of the agreement rather than at the moment of execution. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on fairness and the removal of undue hardship (*haraj*) in commercial and personal status laws. It serves as a foundational text for understanding the conditional nature of *kitabah* (self-purchase) agreements in Islamic jurisprudence.
